  • Build data infrastructure
  • Build custom applications (or help buy and integrate third-party ones)
  • Learn AI engineering and AI usage so that they can do more for themselves

Some of my teams have embedded AI engineers in marketing, recruiting, finance, and other departments. It’s always interesting for engineers to learn about other functions, and those other teams end up with not just better systems but also significantly improved knowledge of AI. In addition, the number of ideas they end up wanting to build always outstrips the capacity of the embedded engineers (because the bottleneck is not coding, but product management, workflow redesign, and other tasks such as judgement tasks, which still take a significant amount of human effort).

Looking across many businesses, the opportunities for AI engineers to make a difference seem endless. I write this from Silicon Valley, where people who are skilled in AI engineering are in great demand. As AI adoption spreads, I expect global demand for people with AI engineering skills to keep growing.

Keep building!

Andrew

P.S. To build your AI engineering skills, please consider joining me and 2000 other AI engineers and builders in person at AI Dev in New York City, November 30th-December 1st! We have a great speaker lineup including Yann LeCun and many others. Get tickets here: AI Dev at DeepLearning.AI

A MESSAGE FROM DEEPLEARNING.AI

Where is your next AI engineer hire coming from? Entry-level tech jobs now demand AI skills, and most college courses haven’t caught up. At AI Dev NYC, Brendan Collins and Aankit Patel share how the city is putting AI engineers in the classroom to close the gap. Readers of The Batch get an exclusive 20 percent off.

News

Gemini Leads the Pack Again

Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon puts the company on top of Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, edging past Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, while costing less per task. As with Gemini 4 Argon, Google is making Carbon available to select cybersecurity companies ahead of general availability.

What’s new: Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon, a multimodal model that it says is designed for cybersecurity tasks. There is no set date for Carbon’s wider release.

  • Input/output: Text, image, speech, and video in (up to 1 million tokens), text out (94.6 tokens per second)
  • Features: Adjustable reasoning
  • Performance: First on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index v5.0 (59), second on Vals AI’s Vals Index v2.2 (70.36 percent), first on Arena.ai’s Text leaderboard (1,528 Elo)
  • Availability: A small set of Google-selected companies, with access expanding gradually to other companies in its Fairwind Program
  • Price: Via API at an introductory price of $2/$0.10/$10 per million input/cached/output tokens, then $4/$0.20/$20 per million input/cached/output tokens
  • Weights/license: Proprietary
  • Undisclosed: Parameter count, architecture, training data and methods, knowledge cutoff, end date of introductory pricing, date for broader availability

How it works: Google says Gemini 4 Carbon builds on Gemini 4 Argon, which it described as a mixture-of-experts model trained via reinforcement learning on reasoning, problem-solving, and theorem-proving data. The company says it worked to improve Carbon in coding, science, multistep agentic tasks, full-stack web development, and multimodal understanding. Carbon shares Gemini 4 Argon’s safety measures, including resistance to prompt injection and adversarial prompts. The company also filtered Argon and Carbon’s training data to remove sexual abuse material, personally identifiable information, and pages from low-trust websites.

Performance: Gemini 4 Carbon ranks first on Artificial Analysis’ recently updated Intelligence Index v5.0 and second on Vals AI’s Vals Index. It leads most tests of expert knowledge and factual recall but trails Claude Opus 5.5 on Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index.

  • On Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, a weighted average of nine tests of knowledge work, coding, science, and general knowledge, mostly using private test sets, Gemini 4 Carbon set to high reasoning ranks first (59, $7.76 and 21.6 minutes per task), ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. It costs less per task than Claude Opus 5.5, but more than GPT-6 Astra.
  • Carbon ranks first on four of the nine individual Intelligence Index tests: AutomationBench-AA, which measures performance on business tasks; HLE-Diamond, expert-level academic questions revised from Humanity’s Last Exam; Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, research tasks in the sciences carried out in a terminal; and AA-Omniscience v1.1, which measures general knowledge against hallucination rates.
  • On Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index v2.0, which tests combinations of models and harnesses on three coding benchmarks, Gemini 4 Carbon set to high reasoning running in Google’s Antigravity CLI ranks second (59, $7.74 and 29.8 minutes per task). It trails Claude Opus 5.5, but Carbon costs less per task and finishes faster.
  • On Vals AI’s Vals Index v2.2, eight finance, coding, legal, and tax benchmarks weighted by each sector’s share of U.S. gross domestic product, Gemini 4 Carbon set to high reasoning ranks second (70.45 percent accuracy, $10.51 and 47.75 minutes per task), trailing only Claude Sonnet 5.5 set to max reasoning, while again costing less and finishing faster.
  • On Arena.ai’s Text Arena leaderboard, which ranks models via blind head-to-head comparisons, Gemini 4 Carbon ranks first (1,528 Elo), ahead of Gemini 4 Argon and Claude Opus 5.5.
  • Gemini 4 Carbon leads all models on three challenging cybersecurity benchmarks: CWE-bench (71.0%), ExploitGym (54.8%), and SEC-bench Pro (88.2%). These scores are self-reported.

Behind the news: Gemini 4 Carbon arrived around two weeks after Google made Gemini 4 Argon broadly available, and just a day after Artificial Analysis revised its Intelligence Index. The updated Index swaps in more demanding tests and splits the score evenly among knowledge work, coding, science, and general knowledge. Models’ scores on version 5.0 don’t compare directly with those of earlier versions. For example, Kimi 3.1 Pro, the best-performing open weights model, was just three points behind Claude Opus 5.5 using the old Index; now it is 12 points behind Claude Opus 5.5 and 13 points behind Gemini 4 Carbon.

Why it matters: Once Gemini 4 Carbon’s introductory discount ends, it will cost exactly what Claude Opus 5.5 costs per token. Yet on Artificial Analysis’ Index, it finishes tasks with 29 percent fewer output tokens and costs 23 percent less per task. As frontier models converge on price and score, token efficiency becomes an increasingly competitive feature.

We’re thinking: Google CEO Sundar Pichai introduced Gemini 4 Carbon by reminding followers that he’d said Google would release models “periodically.” Two frontier models within a few weeks is an impressive pace. Gemini 4 Carbon’s 9-point lead over Gemini 4 Argon on Artificial Analysis’ index shows that frequent releases can bring big gains. We hope Google maintains this rapid rhythm.

Anthropic Pursues A Public Offering

Claude’s maker will sell company shares to the public for the first time. Anthropic’s financial statements show first-half revenue that grew 14-fold from a year earlier, an operating profit in the second quarter, and $895 billion in commitments to buy computing power.

What’s new: On October 26, Anthropic filed an S-1, the registration statement a company must submit to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission before it goes public. Anthropic plans to list on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker ANT. According to the filing, the offering’s main purposes are to increase Anthropic’s capital and financial flexibility and to create a public market for its shares. Anthropic plans to use the money to support its continued growth, including much-needed compute and infrastructure.

The offering: Anthropic could go public as soon as the week before Thanksgiving and hopes to sell roughly $100 billion in shares, according to The Wall Street Journal. The filing leaves the final share price and total share count blank. Some investors expect Anthropic’s post-IPO valuation to land between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion, according to Bloomberg.

Who’s in charge: Public shareholders will get almost no say in the company’s future direction. A single share held by a company owned by Anthropic’s seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, carries 50.1 percent of the vote on most matters, and its voting power will automatically remain at 50.1 percent if Anthropic issues more stock.

The numbers: Anthropic’s revenue is growing much faster than its spending, even accounting for the growing cost of compute.

  • Revenue reached $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion a year earlier. Anthropic says it doesn’t expect revenue to keep growing quite that fast. In 2026’s second quarter, Anthropic earned an operating profit (revenue minus the costs of running the business) of $974 million on $11.6 billion in revenue, its first in any period the filing reports.
  • The company’s quarterly compute and infrastructure expenses rose from $944 million in early 2025 to $5.6 billion in the second quarter of 2026, but compute and infrastructure’s share of revenue fell from 251 percent to 48 percent.
  • Under standard accounting rules, Anthropic lost $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, but most of that came from an accounting adjustment, not money the company spent. Day-to-day operations brought in $3.9 billion in cash.
  • Anthropic has committed to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on computing power, often with companies that also finance it. Named deals include about $161.2 billion in rent on equipment from the chipmaker Broadcom, at least $114.5 billion with Google, at least $110 billion with Amazon, and up to $120.5 billion with SpaceXAI, under agreements that either party can cancel after early 2027. Google and Amazon both invested early in Anthropic, a relationship that the S-1 warns could lead to conflicts of interest.
  • The S-1 reveals that Anthropic’s Claude wrote more than 90 percent of the contributions to Anthropic’s codebase in September 2026. However, the filing says that using AI to build more capable AI in this way “could also pose a considerable safety risk.”

Risk disclosures: The S-1 laid out both conventional and unusual risks for a mainstream American technology company.

  • Government sanctions could pose a future risk. In June 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce imposed worldwide export restrictions on Fable 5 and Mythos 5, two configurations of what was then Anthropic’s most capable model. To comply, Anthropic switched off both models for every customer, while its other models stayed available. It restored them once Commerce lifted the restrictions.
  • Disagreements with the Pentagon could cost Anthropic business, including with other government agencies and to companies that sell to the U.S. government. In February, after Anthropic said its technology shouldn’t be used for mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous weapons, the President directed federal agencies to stop using it. The Department of Defense then designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk under two different laws. The final result of the dispute is still pending in court.
  • Like other labs, security lapses during model testing expose the company to potential liabilities. During pre-release cybersecurity tests built by an outside partner, a setup error left models connected to the Internet. Four Anthropic models gained unauthorized access to real third-party computer systems. Anthropic found no evidence that any model pursued goals beyond its assigned task. It suspended some of those tests.
  • The filing also notes concerns, raised inside Anthropic as well as by outside researchers and regulators, that sufficiently advanced AI could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity” without appropriate safeguards.

Why it matters: For developers using Claude, the filing should be more reassuring than alarming. Anthropic held $112.4 billion in cash at the end of June and turned an operating profit in the second quarter, which testifies to the company’s stability. Even export restrictions (the most direct hit to customers so far) proved temporary. Anthropic restored the models once the U.S. government lifted them and released updated versions in September.

We’re thinking: Within just a few years, Anthropic has gone from a promising startup to potentially a trillion-dollar company — kudos to the whole Anthropic team for this tremendous work! Stock valuations aside, Anthropic’s robust financials should help legitimate an industry that some critics have argued is overhyped. We’re less sure what to think about the filing’s risk factors: They’re a mix of sci-fi scenarios and genuine risks with implications that are difficult to forecast. We’re hopeful that public investment will help Anthropic continue to improve its products for years to come — and let their present performance, rather than speculative future scenarios, speak for them.

One successful run does not mean your agent is reliable. In our new course, you’ll read your agent’s traces to find recurring failures, build code evaluators and LLM judges you can trust, and use evals to check that each change makes your agent better. Enroll now

World Models Become Robot Playgrounds

Google says that Genie 4, its latest world model, will be used in tandem with Gemini models to create digital practice spaces for robots, giving them endless worlds to train in. So far, though, Google’s demos suggest there’s still a long way to go.

What’s new: On October 27, Google announced Genie 4, which it has released to a limited group of testers in a research preview. Genie 4 produces interactive worlds that Google says are even more realistic than its predecessor, Genie 3. Users can change a scene midway through with a text prompt, but now Gemini models help work those changes into the scene. Genie 4 also adds sound, which allows it to create real-time audio for each world it generates, whether it’s two people chatting on a motorcycle or snow crunching under a crowned crane’s feet. Google AI Ultra subscribers as well as some developers should be getting access in the weeks ahead.

How it works: Genie 4 doesn’t have a technical report out yet, but Google’s announcement explains how Gemini models can help direct what Genie 4 renders.

  • Navigation: Users move through a scene with video game-style mouse and keyboard controls.
  • Text directions: While Genie 4 renders a scene, Gemini 3.8 Flash works alongside it as a director. It breaks the user’s goal into steps, then double-checks each new frame to make sure each of those steps has been executed, adjusting its plan if the user inserts changes as things go along.
  • Video: Gemini Omni, Google’s video generation model, helps Genie 4 render more realistic scenery. Google demoed examples including a maple seed gracefully spinning and landing on grass, as well as people shuffling along a 1980s-era train platform.
  • Robotics: In a demo, Google’s reasoning model Gemini 4 Argon broke a task into text-based steps for Genie 4 while it rendered a simulation of Apptronik’s Apollo humanoid robot playing checkers with a person. Google didn’t describe a robot control system in the loop.

Results: Google’s announcement was full of curated demos, but the company didn’t offer any quantitative evaluations to back them up. Google says a simulation can run up to two minutes, roughly double Genie 3’s limit, but DeepMind research engineer Hang Qi noted that reaching that limit doesn’t guarantee that a scene will keep its consistency the whole time, according to Bloomberg. Google says it’s still working to improve complex physical interactions. One of its demos even includes a physics slip: A marble bust that drops onto a watermelon settles on its plinth when it should topple over the side. “There’s only so much that you can do with two minutes,” Google DeepMind product manager Diego Rivas said, according to TechCrunch. “We’re still in the research journey. We’re not necessarily in the end product journey.”

Behind the news: Genie 4 has plenty of company. The world models field is getting more crowded, although not every world model operates the same way. Like GWM Worlds 2, the model Runway released in September, Genie 4 generates video in real time. Marble, from AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li’s startup World Labs, and HY-World 2.0, an open-weights model from Chinese tech giant Tencent, build persistent 3D scenes instead. Like AI video companies, more and more world model companies have become robotics companies, or at least are pursuing applications of their models to robotics.

  • Robotics isn’t the only field disrupted by the new wave of world models. When Genie 3 opened to paying subscribers in January, it sparked a sharp selloff of video game stocks. In October, electric-vehicle maker Rivian bought world-model startup Third Dimension to bring self-driving simulation in house.
  • The field is also consolidating. AMD agreed in September to buy World Labs for about $8.2 billion, and Amazon has been in talks to acquire Decart, whose products include world models for robotics and driving simulation, according to The Wall Street Journal.
  • Genie 3 served as an environment for SIMA, DeepMind’s agent for 3D virtual worlds. Waymo later built a driving simulator on Genie 3 to generate unusual scenarios (things like a tornado or an elephant in the road).
  • Runway has also pushed its world models toward robotics. In February, it announced that robot-control policies acting inside a robotics version of its video model earned simulated scores that closely tracked their real-world results in tabletop tests. In September, Runway debuted a research preview of GWM Worlds 2, a real-time world model with audio. It also announced Praxis-1, a model for controlling real robots that it plans to release with open weights.

Why it matters: Google’s clearest evidence that simulation can improve real robots comes from a different approach from other companies. A few weeks before Genie 4’s debut, Google showed Gemini 4 Argon writing physics simulations in the MuJoCo engine based on photos and video. From a single photo of a tabletop, Argon generated more than 4,500 practice episodes, and fine-tuning a robot-control model on them raised its real-world success rate from 56 percent to 75 percent. Google’s proposed path forward, which it calls hybrid world models, would combine elements of both the structured reasoning of language and code models with a generative model that renders pixels. Theoretically that could give generated environments reliable cause and effect, which is something video models often lack.

We’re thinking: A good robot simulator lets plans fail, since robots learn from mistakes as well as successes. Genie 4 pairs its renderer up with a Gemini director that checks whether each step of a plan succeeded. This can accidentally drift the world toward whatever the intended outcome is. In the marble bust clip, the model itself seems to choose a neat landing on the plinth instead of the toppling over the side like physics says it should. Our question for DeepMind: Can a plan fail in Genie 4? We’d like to see that Apptronik robot hand mess up and drop a few checkers, too.

Context Engineering for Images

Managing an agent’s context by storing all the input text it receives and giving it tools to search the text boosts its performance. For vision-language agents, the same is true of storing images.

What’s new: Qiushi Han, Keya Hu, Linlu Qiu, and colleagues at MIT released VISTA, an agent that completed the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark of interactive visual-reasoning puzzles using 57.4 percent fewer actions than humans who had not encountered them before. The VISTA harness is freely available under the MIT license.

Key insight: Given an image frame from a videogame or other interactive environment, agentic systems typically embed it and keep the embedding until the context is full, at which point they delete it. This raises two issues: Embeddings are lossy and may not retain valuable information, and once an embedding has been deleted, the model no longer has access to information it contained. Storing all frames in a persistent memory retains all the information they carry, and enabling an agent to retrieve and zoom in on them makes it possible to embed details that otherwise may not have been captured.

How it works: VISTA works with Anthropic Claude Opus 5.0 or OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol. Its harness works similarly to other popular harnesses, except it retains all input frames and includes a tool that retrieves frames. Given a new frame and list of available keyboard actions (such as left, right, up, down, spacebar, or click), the agent tells the model to decide whether to (i) read or update notes, (ii) retrieve previous frames, (iii) retrieve previous actions and their results, or (iv) execute an action. It repeats this choice until the model takes action. After the environment updates (during which it may produce a series of frames), it adds to the model’s input the last frame and a new list of available actions and executes the loop again.

  • The agent maintains two notes: information it deduces about the environment that can be reused across levels or sessions (for example, the difference between a brown block and a black background), and information deduced about the level or problem at hand (for example, that the character currently has a power-up or conditions under which the model failed previously). The agent decides when to read these notes.
  • When the agent decides to retrieve earlier frames, the tool enables it to retrieve any number of frames and zoom in to any part of a frame.
  • During an attempt to complete a puzzle or game level, VISTA stores in memory not only images but also a list of actions and their results. It can decide to retrieve any set of previous actions or summaries of all previous attempts.

Results: The authors tested VISTA on ARC-AGI-3 (25 games), GameWorld (170 tasks in 34 games), and AI GameStore (10 games). It enabled Claude Opus 5.0 and GPT-5.6 Sol to outperform earlier agents as well as humans who encountered the same challenges for the first time.

  • On ARC-AGI-3, VISTA with Claude Opus 5.0 achieved a perfect score of 100 Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), meaning it completed all puzzles in fewer actions than first-time human players. (Earlier projects that achieved perfect RHAE scores, such as Tycho, generated programs that simulated the environments.) VISTA with GPT-5.6 Sol achieved 99 RHAE. Denied the ability to store frames, VISTA with GPT-5.6 Sol achieved 70 RHAE, which shows that the frames were useful.
  • On GameWorld, VISTA with GPT-5.6 Sol completed 63.3 percent of tasks on average. First-time human players completed 55.3 percent, and the native harness with GPT-5.6 Sol completed 40 percent.
  • On AI GameStore, VISTA with GPT-5.6 Sol achieved a much higher score than first-time players and the native harness, 40 percent better than humans on average.

Why it matters: Games and other interactive environments generate potentially endless streams of frames, each of which contain information an agent may not have deduced earlier. Only so many frames fit in its context, and not all frames are relevant at any given moment. By storing all frames and giving the agent tools to retrieve them, agents can find the relevant frames and re-examine them within the current context.

We’re thinking: Apparently context engineering helps whether the medium is text or images. Multimodal systems benefit from multimodal context management.

articles.title: GPT-6 Cyber Versus Linux, The Problem With LLM-Powered Search, LLMs Edit Model Weights, Agentic Doc Retrieval
articles.content_html:
Dear friends,

Building an agent harness has been a rapidly growing method to build an AI agent. The OpenWorker project just released the open source OpenWorker Agent Harness SDK, which I invite you to check out. If you have not built an agent harness before, I encourage you to do so. (This skill is reflected in the AI Engineering Skills Map, and job interviews increasingly ask people if they’ve done this.) This letter describes how to steer coding agents to quickly build an agent harness.

An agent harness is the code that wraps around an LLM and provides it with context, tools, and guardrails to turn it into an application. Since late last year, LLMs have become powerful enough that it’s practical to build many applications by repeatedly calling an LLM and letting it decide what to do next. For example, you might build your own coding agent by giving it tools (functions) to read/save files, run shell commands, execute code the agent has written, and read output of the executed code. Given these tools, you can build a simple coding agent that can save code to a file, run it, see if there are any errors, and iterate to improve the code.

To take a second example, here’s how you can build a simple demo agent that organizes files. First, in a new/empty project directory, run in bash:

npx @openworkerai/openworker-harness-builder --agent claude --project . 

Replace “claude” above with “codex” if your coding agent is Codex. This should install OpenWorker’s openworker-harness-builder in the current directory. Then, prompt your coding agent with a prompt like:

Use the openworker-harness-builder skill to build a small local file-organizing agent using the OpenWorker Harness SDK. Generate 10 sample text files in a dedicated demo directory. The app should have an agent that has tools to list and read files, create/delete subdirectories, and move files. Configure the harness such that all of these tools are restricted to only the demo directory. Use OPENAI_API_KEY in ~/.env and gpt-6.1-terra [or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and claude-sonnet-5-5]. Prompt the agent to organize files, create subdirectories, and move files into appropriate subdirectories to organize the files. Require user approval before each subdirectory creation and file move, showing the proposed operation. Display tool activity so the user can see what happens at each step of the demo. As it is running, also display a succinct description of the status of the agent loop so the user can see what’s happening.

Building an agent harness requires managing LLM context. For long-running agents, this requires building a memory architecture (such as memory compaction when the context gets too long). A harness may also need guardrails (such as input/output checking), a mechanism for approvals, security controls (for example, keeping credentials away from the LLM), and sandboxing. OpenWorker Desktop is finding usage in many security workflows, and Rohit Prsad and I built the OpenWorker Harness SDK to make it easier to improve OpenWorker Desktop. But we were delighted to hear that several other groups found the Harness SDK useful for building other agents, which is why we’re releasing it as open source. You can use it to build agents that run locally or are deployed online.

If you have not yet built an agent harness, please follow the steps above and give it a shot. Unlike the agent harness tools offered by model providers, OpenWorker’s Harness SDK is open source and not beholden to any model, so you can easily build agents that run with any model provider and on any cloud.

Keep building!

Andrew

A MESSAGE FROM DEEPLEARNING.AI

The agenda for AI Dev NYC, November 30 to December1, is live! Hear Yann LeCun and Andrew Ng in conversation, plus sessions by OpenAI, Runway ML, and You.com on production systems, video models, and agent inference. Readers of The Batch get an exclusive 20 percent off

News

GPT-6 Cyber Patches More Security Flaws for Less Cost

OpenAI built a cybersecurity model that discovered, exploited, and patched nearly 950 root-level vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel in a single run.

What’s new: GPT-6 Cyber, a version of GPT-6 Astra fine-tuned to find, exploit, and patch security flaws, is restricted initially to approved customers. In a mid-October scan of the Linux kernel, GPT-6 Cyber addresed 948 flaws that allow ordinary users to gain full control of a machine. The run cost around $1,280 per vulnerability. (In July, the same harness running GPT-5.6 Sol addressed 166 such vulnerabilities for around $3,100 each.)

  • Input/output: Text and images in (up to 1,050,000 tokens), text out (up to 128,000 tokens)
  • Features: Reasoning, tool use, streaming, structured outputs
  • Performance: More capable than GPT-6 Astra on most tests of cybersecurity conducted by OpenAI
  • Availability: Initially offered to selected customers of OpenAI’s Daybreak Red advanced security program; customers must use single sign-on, multifactor authentication, managed devices, and least-privileged access and restrict API requests to specific IP addresses
  • Price: API $20/$2/$100 per million input/cached/output tokens for requests up to 272,000 input tokens, $40/$4/$150 above that; cache writes $25 per million tokens for 30 minutes, $50 per million tokens for 12 hours
  • License: Proprietary
  • Undisclosed: Parameter count, architecture, training data, training details, knowledge cutoff, reasoning levels, schedule for wider availability

How it works: OpenAI fine-tuned GPT-6 Cyber via reinforcement learning on tasks such as reproducing crashes, generating working exploits, and finding code vulnerabilities. The reward function discouraged refusal of authorized security requests and reward hacking, and it encouraged the model to stay within authorized behaviors and to report results accurately. A team of agents ran a pipeline that enabled the model to find, confirm, and exploit flaws in the Linux kernel and patch them.

  • In the pipeline, scout agents identified security-relevant parts of the kernel that ordinary users can reach. Analyst agents read the scout agents’ candidate code and flagged 2,308 flaws within 12 hours. For each candidate, a triage agent wrote a short program to trigger the flaw in a virtual machine that detected memory errors.
  • The triage agent iterated until the flaw appeared or the agent ran out of approaches. This step confirmed 1,724 flaws within 30 hours. A screening agent reviewed the confirmed flaws and kept those that had a plausible path to root access that would confer full control of a machine.
  • Exploit-writing agents tried to gain root access in virtual machines configured with a standard Linux distribution’s protections and produced 1,169 working exploits. The pipeline checked nearby code for variants of each flaw and wrote 948 distinct patches for 948 distinct vulnerabilities. Security researchers reviewed the exploits and proposed severity ratings before reporting them to Linux maintainers.

Performance: GPT-6 Cyber proved substantially more capable than GPT-5.6 Cyber in tests by OpenAI, and it outperformed GPT-6 Astra on most benchmarks.

  • On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability in a remote target, GPT-6 Cyber set to the highest reasoning level tested (48.45 percent) outperformed GPT-6 Astra set to its highest level (42.43 percent) and GPT-5.6 Cyber (32.1 percent). On a version of ExploitGym with stronger defenses, GPT-6 Cyber (36.94 percent) outperformed GPT-6 Astra (29.69 percent). Gemini 4 Carbon, evaluated by Google without guardrails at an undisclosed reasoning level, achieved 54.8 percent.
  • ExploitGym Honeypot gives a model a hard exploitation task alongside a supporting service it may use but isn’t authorized to attack. Without OpenAI’s deployment safety instructions, GPT-6 Cyber attacked the supporting service in 0.07 percent of attempts, compared with 5.51 percent for GPT-5.6 Cyber and 49.5 percent for GPT-5.6 Sol. With the instructions in place, OpenAI observed no attempts by GPT-6 Cyber. (GPT-6 Astra, without specialized security training, attacked in 0 percent of attempts.)
  • On FrontierCyber, 288 real-world challenges, GPT-6 Cyber solved 90 and GPT-6 Astra solved 96. Neither model solved any of the 15 hardest challenges, nor did they successfully attack a fully hardened target.

Behind the news: The cybersecurity capabilities of recent top-performing AI models — which are available either in guardrailed versions or to selected customers — have set security personnel on high alert. In October, the U.S. government warned of critical flaws in the PHP scripting language after researchers working with OpenAI had reported them. Hackers stole $6.3 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, the biggest known crypto heist, in an exploit that involved compromised internal AI tools.

Why it matters: The latest cybersecurity models pose both challenges and opportunities for security. On one hand, they’re extremely adept at exploiting flaws. On the other, they make flaws easy and inexpensive to find and fix. The hacking competitions Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN have offered $20,000 and $70,000 respectively per Linux kernel exploit. GPT-6 Cyber wrote them for a small fraction of that cost and proposed patches to boot.

We’re thinking: In the honeypot test, the rate at which the model attacked an unauthorized target fell from 49.5 percent (GPT-5.6 Sol) to 5.51 percent (GPT-5.6 Cyber) to 0.07 percent (GPT-6 Cyber), and to nothing once the deployment instructions were in place. That is a steep rate of improvement!

LLMs Can Fine-Tune Neural Networks

Research suggests that you can improve a neural network’s weights simply by prompting an LLM — for networks of less than 1 billion parameters, at least.

What’s new: Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, and colleagues from MIT showed that GPT-6 Astra can interpret, improve, and produce neural network weights in proof-of-concept studies.

How it works: The authors asked GPT-6 Astra to (a) identify which game a network was trained on based on its weights, (b) alter the weights of a network to improve its ability to operate a simulated car, and (c) generate a network that would win a game. In a more practical experiment, they asked GPT-6 Astra to improve Qwen3.5-0.8B’s math performance.

  • The authors built grid versions of Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway and trained a separate copy of the same small network (a 17,253-parameter vanilla neural network) on each. Given the weights and asked “Which game was this neural network trained on?” GPT-6 Astra named the game correctly in all four cases.
  • The authors used PPO to train a 171,664-parameter vanilla neural network to drive a car up a ramp in the Kinetix environment, and it never succeeded in 256 episodes. They gave GPT-6 Astra the scene, the goal, the network’s weights, and one recorded episode of the failure, and asked it to explain the cause and fix only that, in a single reply with no tools and no way to run the network. Astra edited 3.5 percent of the weights, and the car succeeded in all 1,024 episodes.
  • They gave GPT-6 Astra the rules and source code of a game (Breakout, Seaquest, or Asterix, from the MinAtar suite) and a small network of about 20,000 parameters with every weight set to 0, and asked it to write weights that would play. For comparison they trained networks of the same size using PPO. Astra’s networks outscored PPO at 100 million training steps in all three games, and in Breakout scored 517.4 against 25.3 at 500 million steps. Of the three games, Astra led on one, roughly tied on one, and lost on the third.
  • GPT-6 Astra, given Qwen3.5-0.8B’s weights, a tool to run it, and practice problems from the GSM8K and MATH-500 training sets, was asked to improve its benchmark performance. It found that Qwen3.5-0.8B often looped, filling its context window unnecessarily, and modified 0.016 percent of the weights. The change boosted performance on MATH-500 from 7.9 percent to 48.1 percent.

Yes, but: Not all case studies yielded positive results. Asking GPT-6 Astra to improve Gemma 3 270M’s math performance didn’t work. Astra found ordinary mistakes in its reasoning, wrong arithmetic and invalid algebra, but no single component responsible for them that it could switch off, and its edits barely moved the model’s MATH-500 performance.

Why it matters: These results are proofs of concept that have not been shown to extend to more diverse LLMs and target models. However, they show how LLMs could be used in building models. They might improve interpretability, enabling us to better understand the networks we build. Or they might facilitate network editing or generation, making it possible to diagnose and fix obvious issues or accelerate training.

We’re thinking: If editing weights directly works at larger scales, it could change how models are improved. The authors achieved their improvements without a single gradient step.

Enable agents to make reliable predictions on tabular data. In “Tabular Foundation Models for Data Science Agents,” you’ll give a pretrained model your data plus its training examples as context. Then you’ll build an agent that calls it as a tool to make predictions. Enroll for free

Search Engine Wars, LLM Update

Google is turning its search engine into a chatbot, and OpenAI is turning its chatbot into a search engine. Yet neither company has made AI-powered search bring in as much revenue per query as traditional search.

What’s new: Alphabet, Google’s parent company, reported a 25 rise in revenue between July and September. However, its search revenue growth slowed to 12 percent, down from 19 percent and 17 percent in the previous two quarters — despite a rising tide of search queries — as it tries to use large language models to improve the search experience. Meanwhile, OpenAI’s business expanded, presumably including many queries that once would have been entered into a conventional search engine. An OpenAI executive said ChatGPT’s weekly users had grown from 1 billion to 1.2 billion in two months, and it claims to handle roughly one-fifth as many searches as Google.

How Google search pays: Google makes money when advertisers pay for their messages to appear beside search results, but that business is slowing.

  • Google collected $63.35 billion from traditional search and related ads from July through September, including ads in its LLM-powered AI Overviews and AI Mode. The number of queries it received grew at its fastest rate in five years.
  • Google didn’t reveal how much of that revenue came from AI Mode, but an AI Mode query brings in less revenue than a comparable traditional search, because it shows fewer ads and advertisers pay less for them, Ars Technica wrote. In effect, Google’s LLMs are cannibalizing its search revenue.

How AI search ads work: Meanwhile, both Google and OpenAI are pushing ads into LLM-generated search results.

  • On the day it issued its financial report, Google said AI Mode will show ads in 11 countries, up from 1 previously. In the U.S., ads will appear when a user enters a follow-up query.
  • OpenAI, which began to test ads early this year, now shows them in 89 countries to users of ChatGPT’s free and low-cost Go plans. OpenAI says its ad sales reached a pace of $1 billion per year within 200 days of launch, a figure that hasn’t been verified independently. That works out to about $250 million every three months, compared with Google’s $63.35 billion.

Yes, but: OpenAI is a private company, so it’s impossible to assess how much of Google’s search business ChatGPT actually has taken, and estimates vary widely. When it said it processed one-fifth the number of searches Google does, it didn’t explain which Google figure it compared against, Search Engine Journal noted. In February, the search-marketing firm Ahrefs estimated 12 percent, using a different definition of search.

Behind the news: While Google and OpenAI compete for LLM-powered search, the web publishers whose pages LLMs use to generate search results are seeking more control over how AI companies use their work. One proposal would let them put a flag on their pages that would ask AI developers not to use them to train LLMs. Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic said they plan to honor the flag. Meanwhile, Google offers publishers a way to exempt their pages from AI Overviews and AI Mode.

Why it matters: LLMs have many uses, but it’s not yet entirely clear how to build highly profitable businesses on them. LLM-powered search could be one answer, since advertisers already pay to reach users through search engines. Ironically, LLM-powered search is drawing more people, and faster, than it’s drawing advertising money. But until ads in LLM-powered results earn as much as the traditional ads they replace, relying purely on LLM-powered search for revenue isn’t a surefire way to replicate Google’s previous success.

We’re thinking: Chatbots may eventually eat into users’ web searches, but the users themselves won’t necessarily be human. AI agents carrying out tasks such as shopping on a user’s behalf will also see ads that could sway their behavior or recommendations to users. In fact, Time magazine already sells ads aimed at agents instead of people.

Retrieval for RAG-Resistant Docs

Retrieving documents chunk by chunk works well with many types of text, but it can fail with documents in which the meaning of a given span — say, numbers in a table — depends on particulars found elsewhere on the page — say, the label of their units. Researchers assigned agents to keep all the necessary information in view.

What’s new: Sagar Tamang, Ayush Vyas, and Tabarakul Hazarika at Indian Institute of Technology Patna and TwoSpoon, an independent tech lab, developed Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search (READ). Their method replaces vector-based retrieval with an agentic harness and specialized search tools.

Key insight: For RAG-style retrieval, a document is divided into chunks that are embedded, and a model retrieves chunks whose embeddings are similar to the embedding of the query. But this approach can fail with documents such as financial or scientific reports, where numbers in a table gain important meaning from units or dates that may lie many lines away, or legal briefs, in which words may have special meanings that are defined many paragraphs away. An agent with tools to navigate undivided documents can look beyond predefined chunks.

How it works: The authors used the READ method with Gemini 2.5 Pro.

  • The system had access to three tools: (i) A keyword-search tool returned matching line numbers, (ii) an outline tool listed section headings with line numbers, and (iii) a text-reader tool fetched specific line ranges.
  • Given a query like, “What is the mathematical difference between the Fiscal Deficit and the Revenue Surplus for the year 2024-2025?,” the READ agent activated a loop that generated a search term such as “Fiscal Deficit,” scanned a document for the term, checked matching line(s) against the document outline, and read the text from the table headers to the matching line(s).
  • Within the loop, the model refined its query when it got too many hits, too few hits, or insufficient information to make sense of what it found. Each refinement repeated the loop with a new search term or a new range to be read.

Results: The authors used READ, RAG-style retrieval, and RAG-style retrieval in an agentic loop to answer 51 questions about a 780-page financial report published by the government of Gujarat, India. All systems were based on Gemini 2.5 Pro. READ answered 58.8 percent of the questions correctly, against 15.7 percent for chunk-and-embed retrieval and 27.5 percent for chunk-and-embed inside an agentic loop. BM25, a keyword-ranking method from the 1990s with no model in the retrieval step, answered 51.0 percent, which the authors deem statistically indistinguishable from READ.

Why it matters: Chunk-and-embed retrieval methods tend not to work well with documents in which the meaning of any given passage is not self-contained, such as financial reports, contracts, and regulatory filings. In such cases, letting a model search the whole document is more effective.

We’re thinking: The striking number here is not READ’s 58.8 percent but BM25’s 51.0. On RAG-resistant documents, chunk-and-embed lost to plain keyword search by a wide margin, and the agent’s advantage over keyword search did not clear the authors’ own threshold of significance. Before building an agent, it is worth finding out what a keyword search can do.

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s Nvidia legacy, Claude Fable 5.2 and Anthropic’s IPO, World Labs Releases Atlas to Developers
articles.content_html:
Dear friends,

I was saddened to hear about Jensen Huang resigning from Nvidia last week. Yes, Jensen made serious mistakes. At the same time, he is a brilliant leader that has done tremendous work growing AI — providing compute to power training and inference, championing open source, and more — while turning Nvidia into one of the most valuable companies in the world.

Much has been written about Jensen’s unique contributions. I still remember years ago, when I made my early push to use GPUs for training neural networks. Jensen met this idea with a positive reception, and he provided resources to help my teams at Stanford and Google and — long before it was obvious to most people that this was a good idea — directed Nvidia to shift to serving deep learning workloads. This bold call was one of many that led to Nvidia’s success. I appreciate particularly that, to ensure Nvidia’s success, he focused on building a thriving AI ecosystem that enabled many other teams to flourish.

In many large companies, there is a mantra that no one is irreplaceable. In hindsight, this statement certainly did not apply to Jensen. Nvidia’s board may yet reinstate him as CEO, but if not, I wonder what future contributions he could have made to Nvidia that we will miss out on — and never know we missed.

I hope everyone will see in Jensen’s critical role a refutation of the idea that people are replaceable. We should try to build teams that are robust enough to survive any individual’s departure. But at the same time, we should try to make contributions that others will look back on and understand were indispensable.

Jensen is a hero of the AI world. When I wrote the blurb for his TIME 100 Award, I remember thinking there was so much more I could have written about him than would fit in the word count. I’m confident he will continue to make huge contributions. Let us all take inspiration from his example of the difference a single person can make and strive to contribute as much as we can.

Keep building!

Andrew

News

Jensen Huang Resigns as Nvidia CEO

Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s relationship with a possible asset for China’s intelligence agency threw the GPU giant into turmoil, leading to Huang’s apologetic resignation and the Nvidia board’s appointments of Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and Harvey Jones as its first chairman. The scandal brought renewed attention to Nvidia’s central role as a funder of and supplier to the global AI ecosystem, along with China-based companies’ access to advanced AI chips.

What’s new: Jensen Huang had an intimate relationship with Huang Le, who is also known as Alice Huang (the two are unrelated) as early as 2023. Ms. Huang held a high position at Megaspeed, a Singaporean company that supplies processing power to Chinese AI companies. Unusually, U.S. intelligence personnel concluded in 2025 that Ms. Huang was passing information to China, but did not provide a defensive briefing to Mr. Huang or Nvidia, which is typical practice when U.S. citizens or companies are known targets of a foreign intelligence service. After allegations that Ms. Huang was a spy were published in The New York Times, Nvidia’s board of directors announced an independent investigation into the matter. A relationship with an employee also came to light, and Mr. Huang resigned. There are no indications that Jensen Huang knew that Ms. Huang was a spy.

How it works: Nvidia designs the most capable chips for training and running AI. The U.S. government restricts exports of Nvidia’s most capable products to China, but the policy has proven porous: the company’s latest chips can legally reach Southeast Asia, where data centers like Megaspeed’s serve China-based customers. Jensen Huang has opposed export restrictions throughout, arguing that their main effect is to push China to build its own chip industry. Eventually, Nvidia and the Trump administration reached a compromise: Nvidia could sell some of its H200 chips directly to China, while the U.S. would charge a 25 percent export tariff. Exports of Nvidia’s most powerful B200 and B300 GPUs would still be barred to China. But China moved to block U.S. chip imports, claiming that Nvidia GPUs could enable U.S. spying. Instead, China has pressed its own chip designers and fabricators to build domestic substitutes.

  • Between June 2024 and February 2026, a Megaspeed affiliate in Malaysia spent $4.8 billion on Nvidia chips and other AI infrastructure, The New York Times reported. In late 2024, the U.S. Commerce Department investigated a Megaspeed site in Malaysia and found Nvidia chips still in their boxes, as though staged for shipment elsewhere. Nvidia later said it had reviewed the situation and found no evidence to support suspicions that Megaspeed was evading U.S. restrictions.
  • Speculations about Ms. Huang’s role were published in 2025. Megaspeed claimed that Ms. Huang left the company in August of that year. She is believed to have left Singapore and returned to Beijing at that time. In mid-2025, the U.S. government probed Megaspeed on suspicion that it had diverted chips to China, claims both Nvidia and Megaspeed denied. At this time, Nvidia said it stopped selling Megaspeed chips. Nvidia also stopped separately reporting GPU sales to Singapore.
  • Also in 2025, U.S. government officials learned of Jensen Huang’s relationship with Huang Le. In spring 2026, a top-secret memo circulated among senior officials, including President Trump, asserting that China’s Ministry of State Security had recruited Ms. Huang to gather information about Jensen Huang that might help Beijing evade U.S. export restrictions.
  • Reporters at The New York Times made Jensen Huang’s relationship with Huang Le public in late October 2026, along with the charge that Ms. Huang gathered information for Chinese intelligence.
  • On November 11, Nvidia’s board convened an emergency meeting, then announced a CEO transition. Jensen Huang resigned and Colette Kress assumed duties as interim CEO.
  • Less than a week later, Mr. Huang announced that he would resume CEO duties if asked. But newly appointed chair Harvey Jones said on an earnings call for investors that the board had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and did not have plans to reinstate him.

Yes, but: Jensen Huang’s position on selling GPUs to China was established long before his relationship with Ms. Huang. As Nvidia’s CEO, his responsibility was to grow the business, including in the world’s largest market. As an American and Taiwanese citizen, he consistently argued that selling chips to mainland China was good for U.S. and Taiwanese security, since it would make China more dependent on U.S. and Taiwanese technology. Further, he shared this view with many other government and business leaders.

Why it matters: Mr. Huang’s tenure tremendously benefitted the field of AI by providing critical computing technology to developers large and small. The rapid rise of AI put his company at the heart of U.S. national economics and security. Nvidia became the leading supplier of AI chips, responsible for 90 percent of all semiconductor revenue, and, for a time, the most valuable public company in the world. Nvidia under Huang was among the biggest boosters of open weight AI models, whether through its own Nemotron series, its acquisition of Hugging Face, or support for models outside its own ecosystem. Moreover, Nvidia privately funds Anthropic, OpenAI, and Safe SuperIntelligence; invests in CoreWeave, Nebius, Nokia, and xAI; and provides financial support and equipment for the world’s largest data center projects. Under interim CEO Kress (and a great deal more scrutiny from investors and regulators), Nvidia has promised to be more “disciplined” in its capital investments, signaling that its role as an AI “lender of last resort” might be gradually curtailed.

We’re thinking: Three U.S. administrations have tried to keep advanced semiconductors out of China. The effort is not only ineffective, it’s counterproductive for prosperity worldwide and leads other nations to wonder if some day, too, their access to semiconductors might be curtailed. Promoting openness, interoperability, and encouraging others to use American technology would be a better strategy for the US.

Claude Fable Gets a Price Cut

Anthropic updated its most capable public model and removed safeguards for its private twin, opening Claude Mythos to more organizations that apply for access. Meanwhile, the company began selling shares to the public for the first time at a market capitalization of $1.5 trillion.

What’s new: Anthropic introduced Claude Fable 5.2, which costs 20 percent less per token than Claude Fable 5.1. Claude Mythos 5.2, a version with fewer biology and cybersecurity safeguards, is available only to organizations that Anthropic approves.

  • Undisclosed: Parameter count, architecture, training data and methods
  • Weights/license: Proprietary
  • Price: Via API 8/0.20/$40 per million input/cached/output tokens with cache writes at 10/16 per million tokens for five-minute/one-hour caches and 50 percent off for batched requests; fast mode 16/80 per million input/output tokens
  • Availability: Claude Fable 5.2 via Claude apps on eligible paid plans, Claude Code, Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Claude Models on Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry, with 30-day data retention required; Claude Mythos 5.2 only to organizations approved through Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program or Life Sciences Verification Program
  • Performance: First on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index v5.0.1 (65), Vals AI’s Vals Index (71.31 percent), and ARC Prize’s ARC-AGI-3 in its standard harness (81.2 percent)
  • Knowledge cutoff: June 2026
  • Features: Reasoning always on, with five reasoning levels (low, medium, high, xhigh, max), defaults to high in API and medium in Claude apps and Claude Code; tool use; fast mode, which generates tokens up to 2.5 times faster
  • Input/output: Text and images in (up to 1 million tokens), text out (up to 128,000 tokens, 112 tokens per second)

How it works: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are one model with different safeguards. Anthropic described one change to how it trained the model and several to how it restricts the model’s use.

Another anti-distillation measure, which Anthropic calls “preserved thinking” and now applies to all API accounts rather than only new ones, stops anyone from editing earlier turns of a conversation to extract the model’s reasoning.

  • To deter distillation (training a model on another model’s outputs), Anthropic added protections, such as showing users only a summary of the model’s reasoning. Claude models now screen requests that try to extract these traces. The company says this cuts the data distillers collect by 90 to 99 percent.
  • In Claude Fable 5.2, classifiers block high-risk cybersecurity work such as penetration testing (simulated attacks on a system to find vulnerabilities) and generating exploits. Blocked requests route to older models: Claude Opus 4.8 answers barred cybersecurity requests, and Claude Opus 5 answers barred biology requests and a small set of requests about developing AI models. Anthropic says the cybersecurity and biology classifiers are as robust as Claude Fable 5.1’s but block about 55 percent fewer requests; the company describes these as legitimate requests blocked by mistake.
  • During training, Anthropic limited the model’s progress in two skills that can speed development of AI models: optimizing kernels for AI chips and improving large language model architectures. Anthropic says the model performs at about the level of Claude Opus 5.5 in these areas, and that related skills such as agentic coding, hardware development, and “traditional” machine learning research were not limited.

Performance: Claude Fable 5.2 ranks first on independent intelligence leaderboards from Artificial Analysis and Vals AI, but its cost per task is the highest of any model Artificial Analysis has priced. In Anthropic’s tests, Fable 5.2 improved most (relative to its predecessor) on a test of paid freelance projects.

  • On Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index v5.0.1, a weighted average of nine tests of knowledge work, coding, science, and general knowledge, Claude Fable 5.2 set to max reasoning ranks first (65 points, $26.54 and 40.9 minutes per task), ahead of Gemini 4 Carbon (60 points at $5.48 per task) and Claude Opus 5.5 (59 at $10.04 per task). Claude Fable 5.2 posts the highest score on five of the component tests: HLE-Diamond, a test of reasoning and knowledge, AA-Omniscience v1.1, a test of knowledge versus hallucinations, CritPt v2 (Hard Subset), a test of physics reasoning, Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, a test of scientific research workflows in a computer terminal, and FrontierCode-AA 2.0, a test of software engineering in open-source code repositories.
  • On Vals AI’s Vals Index, which combines eight tests of finance, coding, legal, and tax work, Claude Fable 5.2 set to max reasoning ranks first (71.31 percent accuracy, $17.94 and 43.7 minutes per test), ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 (70.85, $16.18 and 86 minutes per test) and Gemini 4 Carbon (70.45, $10.51 and 47.75 minutes per test). Among individual tests, it ranks first on financial analysis tasks (69.47 percent); financial modeling in spreadsheets (77.38 percent); building apps from plain-language requests (93.77 percent); rebuilding programs from scratch (19.00 percent); and biology data investigations developed by Anthropic (83.70 percent). It ties Claude Opus 5.5 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, 66 long tasks in a computer terminal (65.15 percent), and matches several models with a perfect score on ProofBench v1.1, formally verified math proofs.
  • On Arena AI’s Agent Arena, which ranks models by how they perform in real user sessions based on task success, user satisfaction, and steerability, Claude Fable 5.2 ranks first, ahead of Claude Opus 5.5. It also leads Agent Arena’s coding category (33.17 percent net improvement). On Arena AI’s WebDev leaderboard, which ranks models via blind head-to-head comparisons of websites they build, Claude Fable 5.2 ranks first (1,826 Elo) narrowly ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (1,816 Elo).
  • In Anthropic’s tests on the Remote Labor Index, 240 paid freelance projects in areas such as game development, architecture, and data analysis, Claude Fable 5.2 set to high reasoning produced work that human evaluators judged at least as good as the freelancers’ on 41.3 percent of projects, leading all models with more than twice the success rate of Claude Fable 5.1.

Behind the news: Over successive releases, Anthropic has widened access to its top model and cut its price. In April, Anthropic introduced Claude Mythos Preview only for partners in its Project Glasswing cybersecurity program, at $25/125 per million tokens of input/output. In June, it made Claude Fable 5, a version of Mythos Preview’s successor with added safeguards, generally available at $10/50 per million tokens of input/output, while keeping Claude Mythos 5 for selected partners. In September, Claude Fable 5.1 kept those prices and limited Claude Mythos 5.1 to U.S. cybersecurity and life sciences organizations that Anthropic selected. Claude Fable 5.2 cuts prices again, and organizations can now apply for Claude Mythos 5.2. Anthropic introduced its updated models a day before it began marketing its initial public offering to investors. It expects shares to start trading on November 19.

Why it matters: The type of work Anthropic limited in Claude Fable 5.2 is the same type it showcased to investors. In its initial public offering roadshow video, Anthropic said Claude Mythos, writing or porting almost all of the kernels, ran prompt processing (reading input before generating a response) for one Anthropic model on AMD MI355X GPUs in about three days. Anthropic estimated the same work had taken 6 to 12 months with earlier methods. A company that can move its models quickly to another vendor’s chips has more supplier options, which can lower what the company pays for compute. Notably, Anthropic keeps that ability for itself, while Claude Fable 5.2 users receive only Claude Opus 5.5-level help with the same type of tasks.

We’re thinking: Claude Fable 5.2 is more capable than its predecessor Fable 5.1, but Opus 5.5 remains a strong workhorse, especially for monthly subscribers. Bloggers quickly discovered that not only did Fable usage have its own separate weekly meter, but that using Fable depleted total metered usage much more quickly than the corresponding value of API credits. For example, a Claude Ultra plan ($200 per month) might yield approximately $2500 worth of Opus 5.5 usage (as priced via the API) but only $630 of Fable 5.2 usage.

One successful run does not mean your agent is reliable. Learn to read your agent’s traces to find recurring failures, build code evaluators and LLM judges you can trust, and use evals to check that each change makes your agent better. Enroll now

AMD’s World Model Arrives

World Labs has opened Atlas, its latest world model, to the public, offering developers a self-serve API that lets them turn text prompts into 3D scenes and camera-controllable video that they can then export.

What’s new: After announcing Atlas in September, World Labs released its new model to everyone on November 12. Users can build with its web tools such as Viewfinder, which takes a photo or photos and builds a scene from them, and Chisel, which builds scenes from reference images or written prompts. Atlas also comes with two smaller tools, Relight and Splats to Mesh, that (as the names suggest) relight scenes or convert them to meshes. Devs also get pay-as-you-go API access through prepaid credits, complete with a copy-and-paste prompt that lets an AI coding assistant take them through the setup. Users receive $10 of free API credits and a separate $10 for the web apps to get started.

How it works: World Labs calls Atlas an “omni” world model, but under the hood it’s a multimodal autoregressive diffusion transformer pretrained from scratch to handle text, images, video, and 3D data. It links every image and depth map to a specific camera position that lets it render a scene from various viewpoints consistently.

  • Generating a view costs $0.04 for the first frame and $0.008 for each subsequent frame at 720p (the highest resolution that the API offers). Turning views into refined splats is priced at $5.
  • Atlas can work from a single image and render whatever lies outside the frame, or it can reconstruct a location using overlapping photos — as many as 64 in Viewfinder. As World Labs puts it, passing through “more input images gives Atlas more context: The more it sees, the less it imagines.”
  • Developers chain together API calls to build end-to-end 3D workflows. One estimates camera positions and depth from input photos while another renders novel views or a full video from a single camera path. Then, follow-up calls convert those views into Gaussian splats and the splats into polygon meshes, complete with textures for display or simplified colliders for game engines and simulators.

Performance: On Rapidata’s public leaderboard, Atlas led 19 video and world models at following camera-movement instructions, and human raters favored it in 76.7 percent of head-to-head matchups. In World Labs’ own tests of 3D reconstruction across seven datasets Atlas averaged approximately 12 percent less error than the next-best model, Pi3X, although it didn’t lead on every dataset. There isn’t much independent evidence yet; World Labs hasn’t published a model card or a paper, and no outside group has reproduced its reconstruction results.

Behind the news: World Labs, co-founded by Fei-Fei Li, made its Marble world model public a year ago and later offered it to developers through an API. Atlas builds scenes in the same 3D format as Marble.

  • World Labs’ initial Atlas announcement had a significant focus on building simulated environments to train robots. The November launch leads with web apps and 3D pipelines. Its launch page still lists robotics research and simulation as a use, but the new developer docs don’t mention robotics.
  • In September 2026, AMD agreed to acquire World Labs in an all-stock deal valued at about $8.2 billion. The deal closed on November 16, and the company named Li AMD’s chief scientist and executive vice president. Neither AMD’s initial announcement nor its closing statement mentions Atlas or says what will happen to World Labs’ products.

Why it matters: Atlas supplies 3D output that developers can use in their own projects elsewhere. Its splats and meshes can go into game engines and Blender, whereas other world models that stream pixels produce only video. Setting exact camera positions gives developers way more control than describing a camera move in a prompt. And since the onboarding is written for coding agents, a developer can ask an agent to build a scene in plain language. But there are trade-offs. Free-tier outputs can’t be used commercially, and the accuracy claims rest mostly on World Labs’ own tests.

We’re thinking: Many of this fall’s most impressive world-model demos (Google DeepMind’s Genie 4, Runway’s GWM Worlds 2) were interactive videos that only a limited few can actually get their hands on. Atlas currently has a leg up on both for a pretty simple reason: it comes with a price list and an export button. Developers find out what a model is useful for by building with it. With Atlas, they can try it out for themselves.

Adaptive Memory Management

Many agents save past experiences as text in an external store, and most search and update such memories using settings the agent’s developer chose by hand, such as the number of memories to retrieve or the schedule for removing them. Researchers developed a method that learns such settings per task and carries what it learns into similar tasks.

What's new: Eric Hanchen, Zhi Zhang, and colleagues at the University of California Los Angeles, the University of Washington, and Northwestern University developed Memory as a Controlled Process (MEMCON). Their approach wraps around an existing memory backend and calls its existing store, retrieve, and forget functions, learning from experience.

Key insight: The best way to use a memory store changes as an agent gains experience. (a) Early in a stream of tasks, the memory store holds few memories of solved tasks, so the similarities between them may be loose. Searching for memories that are similar to the task at hand may mislead a model more than it helps. Rather than ranking memories for similarity, the agent is better served by searching for memories of how it handled tasks of the same type. (b) Later, a reworded query may reveal something new. (c) As the memory store grows, it’s helpful to remove memories, because they compete for a limited number of retrieval slots. If a task ends with a signal of success or failure, the system that manages the memory can score the decisions involved. The system can sort tasks into types (say, calculating recommendations or comparing stock prices), and the average score per type can tell the system which setting works best for a particular kind of task.

How it works: The authors used three harnesses (implemented in libraries including Lobster) with three models (GPT-4.1-mini, Claude Sonnet-4, and DeepSeek-V3.2) to execute tasks on the web and in simulated environments. They wrapped existing memory backends (such as G-memory) with a small controller that kept a table of scores, one for each pairing of situation and a memory operation (such as retrieve or remove), and updated the scores after every task based on whether the agent had succeeded. Each time the agent was about to fetch from memory, the controller first extracted a compact state representation. It combined what was happening in the task, such as the kind of goal (as specified in the benchmark, like comparing stock prices) and whether the agent was repeating an action, with the state of the memory store, such as roughly how much it held (five possible bins) and whether a successful run from an earlier similar task existed.

  • It picked an operation from the choices including searching memory, searching again with a reworded query, retrieving the successful run from a similar task, merging duplicate entries in the memory store, removing an entry, and skipping the search. It favored the one with the best score so far (the authors had hand-picked sensible default numbers for first time pairings) with an increase toward operations it had tried least often.
  • The controller ran the chosen operation and added whatever came back to the model’s prompt.
  • When a task ended, the controller scored how well it went (based on the outcome and how many steps the agent took to achieve it). It considered the memory choices it had made during that task and updated its table of scores. Choices made near the end, when the outcome was almost settled, resulted in the greatest increases or decreases. Choices made early got less, since later choices had room to correct them.

Results: The authors compared MEMCON to other memory-management approaches using six benchmarks: three in which an agent acts step by step in a simulated environment, such as ALFWorld (household chores), PDDL (planning puzzles based on PlanBench), and ScienceWorld (science experiments); and three in which it browses the web and uses tools to answer a single question, such as TriviaQA (trivia), WebWalkerQA (navigating websites), and GAIA (assistant tasks that call for tools and documents). MEMCON consistently achieved higher success rates while reducing token consumption. For instance:

  • On ALFWorld, using a Lobster harness and GPT-4.1-mini, MEMCON (67.9 percent success) outperformed the strongest baseline, G-Memory (59.7 percent success). It reduced average input token consumption from 45,000 to 39,000 tokens per task, a 13 percent saving.
  • On GAIA, using a Lobster harness and GPT-4.1-mini, MEMCON (22.4 percent accuracy), outperformed the strongest baseline, G-Memory (21.2 percent accuracy).

Why it matters: An adaptive memory-management layer improves LLM agent performance by giving it the data it needs while reducing computational overhead. The savings and gains came from MEMCON learning to skip or shorten retrieval when retrieval would not help, and to fetch more or retrieve a successful run when retrieval would help, so it spent fewer tokens on irrelevant text while finding more useful memories.

We’re thinking: One common way to optimize agentic behaviors is through training, another is through calls to the underlying model. This work suggests that a lightweight algorithm for adaptive memory management can be simpler and cheaper.

articles.title: GPT-5.5 Outperforms (and Hallucinates), Kimi K2.6 Leads Open LLMs, AI Strains Climate Pledges, Strategic Thinking in LLMs vs. Humans
articles.content_html:
Dear friends,

The ways we prompt AI are very different in 2026 than 2022 when ChatGPT came out. Some people are still using LLMs primarily by asking them short questions. But the models can do much more, like think for minutes, ingest many documents as context, and use web search and other tools.

I’m teaching a new course, AI Prompting for Everyone, to help everyone become an AI power user — whatever their current skill level — and prompt LLMs to take advantage of their latest capabilities.

The course covers skills that apply to ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and other AI tools:

  • How to use deep research mode for well-researched reports on complex questions.
  • How to give AI the right context, including more documents and images than most people realize they can provide.
  • When to ask AI to think hard for several minutes on important decisions like what car to buy, what to study, or what job to take.
  • How to use AI to generate images, analyze data, and build simple games and websites.

I also cover intuitions about how these models work under the hood, so learners know when to trust their output and when not to. Along the way: you’ll see flying squirrels, a creativity test, some of my old family photos, and fireworks.

Please join me! The course assumes no technical background, so please share it with friends or family who could benefit.

Keep prompting!

Andrew

A MESSAGE FROM DEEPLEARNING.AI

Learn how to get more accurate answers, better writing, and more useful outputs from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. Taught by Andrew Ng, this course covers finding information, brainstorming, and building simple apps. Enroll today

News

GPT-5.5 Outperforms, Hallucinates

The latest update of OpenAI’s flagship model sets new states of the art in important benchmarks but has difficulty distinguishing between what it does and doesn't know.

What’s new: GPT-5.5 is a closed vision-language models that’s built for agentic coding, computer use, and knowledge work. GPT-5.5 Pro is the same model but processes reasoning tokens in parallel during inference. OpenAI set the API prices at roughly double the per-token rates of GPT-5.4.

  • Input/output: Text and images in (up to 1 million tokens via API, 400,000 tokens in Codex), text out (up to 128,000 tokens)
  • Features: Five levels of reasoning (xhigh, high, medium, low, none), tool use, web search, structured outputs, tool search (API only, loads tools on demand rather than all at once), Fast mode (Codex only, generates tokens 1.5 times faster at 2.5 times the price)
  • Performance: Tops Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and ARC-AGI-2
  • Availability/price: GPT-5.5 available in ChatGPT with Plus, Pro, Business, or Enterprise subscription and in Codex for those tiers plus Edu and Go; GPT-5.5 Pro available in ChatGPT with Pro, Business, or Enterprise subscription: GPT-5.5 API $5/$0.50/$30 per million tokens of input/cached/output, GPT-5.5 Pro API $30/$180 per million tokens of input/output with no cached discount
  • Undisclosed: Architecture, parameter count, training data and methods

How it works: OpenAI disclosed few details about how it built GPT-5.5. As is typical of high-performance models, the training data was a mix of publicly available data scraped from the web, licensed from partners, and collected from users and human trainers. The model was trained via reinforcement learning to reason before responding.

Performance: GPT-5.5 generally delivers top performance in objective benchmarks, especially in tests of knowledge, agentic tasks, and abstract visual reasoning. However, it falls behind competitors on subjective evaluations. It’s also more likely to confidently deliver incorrect output.

  • GPT-5.5 set to xhigh reasoning tops the indepedent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, a composite of 10 tests of economically useful tasks, with a score of 60 points. Claude Opus 4.7 set to max reasoning and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview set to reasoning are tied at 57 points.
  • On ARC-AGI-2, visual puzzles that test abstract reasoning, GPT-5.5 set to xhigh (85.0 percent at $1.87 per task) displaced the previous leader Gemini 3 Deep Think (84.6 percent at $13.62 per task) at a substantially lower cost per task.
  • In OpenAI’s tests, GPT-5.5 set state-of-the-art scores on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (command-line workflows that require planning and tool use), OSWorld-Verified (autonomous operation of real computer interfaces), and Tau2-bench Telecom (multi-turn customer-service workflows).
  • On AA-Omniscience Accuracy, a knowledge benchmark that rewards factual recall, GPT-5.5 set to xhigh reasoning posted the highest accuracy at 57 percent. However, on the AA-Omniscience Index, which rewards models for answering correctly and acknowledging ignorance but penalizes them for confidently making mistakes, GPT-5.5 set to xhigh reasoning (20 points) ranked third, behind Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (33 points) and Claude Opus 4.7 set to max reasoning (26 points).
  • On Arena.ai’s leaderboards, which rank models by blind head-to-head comparisons, GPT-5.5 falls well behind competitors. Claude Opus models occupy the top spots across most categories. For instance, as of April 27, GPT-5.5-high ranked seventh in Text Arena and ninth in Code Arena WebDev.

Yes, but: GPT-5.5 knows more than its peers, but it answers incorrectly more often and acknowledges ignorance less often. The AA-Omniscience benchmark poses 6,000 expert-level questions across business, law, health, humanities, science/engineering, and software engineering. It includes a “hallucination rate” that is the ratio of wrong answers to the sum of wrong answers, partially wrong answers, and abstentions. By this measure, GPT-5.5 set to high reasoning hit 85.53 percent, notably worse than Claude Opus 4.7 set to max reasoning (36.18 percent) and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview at (49.87 percent). Apollo Research separately found that GPT-5.5 lied about completing an impossible programming task in 29 percent of samples, a significant jump from GPT-5.4’s 7 percent. OpenAI’s internal monitoring of coding-agent traffic showed a similar pattern.

Security implications: OpenAI released results of VulnLMP, an internal evaluation that tests whether a model can develop exploits against widely deployed software. GPT-5.5 undertook multi-day research campaigns and identified potential memory-related vulnerabilities in a variety of targets, but it did not produce an exploit that was confirmed by OpenAI’s evaluation harness. Under OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework, this evidence places GPT-5.5 within the “high” tier of cybersecurity threats, short of the “critical” tier label that would describe models that independently produce working exploits against real targets.

Why it matters: Evaluations of objective performance and human preferences are telling different stories about GPT-5.5. OpenAI regained the lead on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, but the picture flips when it comes to subjective, head-to-head comparisons. Claude Opus models occupy the top spots in LMArena’s Text, Vision, Document, Search, and Code rankings, while GPT-5.5 doesn’t crack the top five on most. Benchmarks measure what models can accomplish, human preference what they’re like to work with. Production decisions usually weigh both, and — according to the measures that are available so far — the two are diverging.

We’re thinking: Top AI companies continue to push the frontier at a dizzying pace. GPT-5.5 is the fourth flagship launch since February, following Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.4, and Google Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview. Each one reshuffled the top of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, which can be viewed as a proxy for general capability in real-world tasks. Developers should design their software stacks to swap models as easily as bumping a dependency.

Big AI’s Plans Strain CO2 Pledges
